characters.name_or_role: Wife (SPEAKER_00, long-nosed woman in brown sweater)
personality_traits: Delivers the opening moralizing line ('We should spend less time on our phones') while never actually looking up from her own phone — establishes her as self-unaware/hypocritical
Passive-aggressive rather than confrontational: her critique of screen time is voiced flatly, not as a real complaint
Domestic, composed presentation (bun hairstyle, pearl earrings, cozy sweater) suggesting a 'together' household image that contrasts with the disconnection being mocked
emotional_range: half-lidded boredom/fatigue (default state, heavy under-eye bags drawn on the felt face)
brief surprise/alertness (eyebrows and mouth open slightly as she starts to speak at 0:00)
returns to flat, glazed-over disengagement almost immediately after speaking
expressions: 0:00 — mouth open, eyebrows slightly raised, mid-sentence delivering the phone line, eyes at half-mast
0:02-0:06 — eyes drop back to phone screen, mouth closes into a flat neutral line, thousand-yard stare
throughout — droopy, heavy-lidded eyes fixed downward at her device rather than at her husband, even while 'discussing' the topic
gestures: holds phone low, close to chest with both hands, thumbs poised to scroll
never turns her whole body toward her husband, only a slight head tilt
static, hunched-forward posture that barely shifts across the whole scene, reinforcing physical inertia matching the phones-not-people theme
characters.interactions_notes: She initiates the conversation topic but does not make eye contact with her husband while speaking or after; her gaze stays locked on her own screen. She is physically adjacent to him on the sofa but there is no real exchange of glances — power dynamic is one of parallel coexistence rather than direct dialogue, visually reinforcing the joke that they are 'together' in name only.

characters.name_or_role: Husband (SPEAKER_00 continues the joke / second voiced line, long-nosed man in glasses and dark robe/coat)
personality_traits: Delivers the punchline ('Modern love is basically sending each other reels from opposite ends of the sofa') in a flat, deadpan register — the comedic 'straight man' who states the absurd truth without irony in his own voice
Visually withdrawn/aloof: sunken, bloodshot-looking eyes and slack downturned mouth suggest chronic under-stimulation or ennui rather than active irritation
Physically the more still and inert of the two — slouched deep into the couch under a blanket-like coat, suggesting comfort with the numbed status quo
emotional_range: flat deadpan through the entire scene — no visible spike in emotion even while delivering the episode's thesis line
faint smirk-adjacent mouth curl (closed, closed-lip near-smile) that reads as resigned amusement rather than joy
brief tightening around the eyes/teeth showing mid-word ('each') that looks almost pained, immediately released back to neutral
expressions: 0:06 — half-lidded eyes look slightly up and away from his phone as he begins the punchline
0:08 — teeth-baring mid-word grimace on 'each', eyebrows knit briefly (close-up shot)
0:09-0:11 — returns to a soft, closed-mouth near-smirk while still holding phone, gaze drifting rather than settling on his wife
gestures: phone held higher and more visibly than his wife's, screen sometimes turned toward camera showing a reels-style feed
arms tucked close to body, minimal movement — sunk into the oversized dark coat which reads as a physical retreat/cocoon
head turns slightly toward his wife only once, right as he says 'each', a small nod-like tilt that acts as his only real acknowledgment of her presence
characters.interactions_notes: He answers his wife's opening statement not with a real response but with a scroll-and-deliver punchline, maintaining the same low engagement she does. The one moment of near eye-contact (his slight head-turn on 'each') is the only physical acknowledgment between them in the whole clip, undercutting the intimacy of the words 'modern love' with visual proof of its absence. Overall dynamic: two people occupying the same frame/sofa without a genuine exchange — the joke's entire visual grammar (parallel poses, synchronized phone-holding, lack of eye contact) is built from their static staging relative to each other rather than any verbal back-and-forth.
